Inspired by the example of Elizabeth of Hungary, she lived simply, and after her husband died on pilgrimage to the Holy Land she gave away her goods to the poor and nursed the sick, including lepers. She became a Franciscan tertiary and moved to Prussia, where in 1260 she enclosed herself in a cell near Kulmsee, praying for the conversion of the people there. She died in the 1260s, and crowds came to her burial. She is remembered as a patron of Prussia.

UO-SIN-001004.name: John before the Latin Gate
UO-SIN-001004.life: John the Apostle, the disciple whom tradition names as the author of the fourth Gospel, is said to have been seized at Rome under the Emperor Domitian. According to tradition, recorded by Tertullian around 200, he was plunged into a vat of boiling oil and came out unharmed, after which he was banished to the island of Patmos, where Revelation was written. A church near Rome's Latin Gate keeps the memory of this story. John is then said to have lived on at Ephesus, guiding the churches there, and to have died peacefully at a great age, the only one of the Twelve not martyred.

UO-SIN-000735.name: John of Beverley
UO-SIN-000735.life: John was born of a noble family at Harpham in Yorkshire and studied at Whitby under Abbess Hilda. He became bishop of Hexham in 687 and bishop of York in 705, and was known as a preacher and a patient teacher. Bede, who was ordained by him, tells how John taught a mute young man to speak, praying over him and then guiding him through letters, syllables and words. John founded a monastery in a woodland at Beverley, and after resigning his see in about 717 he retired there. He died in 721, and Beverley became a great centre of pilgrimage.

UO-SIN-000736.name: Julian of Norwich
UO-SIN-000736.life: Julian lived in Norwich in the late fourteenth century, in a cell attached to the church of St Julian, from which she took her name. At about thirty, in May 1373, she fell gravely ill and received a series of sixteen visions of the sufferings of Christ. She wrote them down at once and spent the following decades reflecting on them, producing the longer Revelations of Divine Love, the earliest surviving book in English by a woman. Writing in a time of plague and unrest, she insisted on the tender love of God and on the hope that "all shall be well." She was still living in 1416.

UO-SIN-000737.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
UO-SIN-000737.life: Gregory was born around 329 in Cappadocia, the son of the bishop of Nazianzus, and studied in Athens, where he formed a lifelong friendship with Basil of Caesarea. He longed for a quiet life of study but was repeatedly drawn into church service. In 379 he was called to Constantinople, then largely Arian, and there preached his Five Theological Orations on the Trinity. He briefly served as bishop of the city but resigned in 381 amid church politics. He retired to Cappadocia, wrote poetry and letters, and died in 390.

UO-SIN-001010.name: Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf
UO-SIN-001010.life: Count Zinzendorf was born in Dresden in 1700 into a noble family with deep Pietist roots. In 1722 he gave refuge on his Saxon estate to persecuted Moravian and Bohemian believers, and the community of Herrnhut grew there. He helped shape the renewed Moravian Church, which organized its life in small groups, and he wrote many hymns. His settlers carried the gospel to the West Indies, Greenland and North America, including Bethlehem in Pennsylvania, which he visited in 1741. Banished from Saxony in 1736, he travelled widely as a kind of pilgrim. He believed that there is no Christianity without community. He died in 1760.

UO-SIN-000739.name: Johann Arndt and Jacob Boehme
UO-SIN-000739.life: Johann Arndt (1555-1621) was a Lutheran pastor who suffered dismissal from one parish for keeping to church images and customs, and later served as superintendent at Celle. His Four Books on True Christianity urged that faith must bear fruit in a renewed life united with Christ, and it was read across Europe. Jakob Boehme (1575-1624) was a shoemaker of Görlitz in Silesia who, after a vision in 1600, wrote on God and creation, beginning with Aurora. Local clergy attacked him and he was forced out of his town, yet his writings influenced later thinkers. Both men are remembered as teachers of inner devotion.

UO-SIN-000740.name: Thomas Rattray
UO-SIN-000740.life: Thomas Rattray was born in 1684, the eldest son of the laird of Craighall in Perthshire, and became a clergyman and scholar in the Scottish Episcopal Church in difficult years when it was cut off from state support. Chosen bishop of Brechin by his fellow clergy in 1727, he became bishop of Dunkeld in 1731 and was elected Primus in 1738. He wrote on the nature of the Church and on the Christian covenant, and he prepared an edition of the ancient Liturgy of St James of Jerusalem. He died in 1743.

UO-SIN-000741.name: Frances Perkins
UO-SIN-000741.life: Frances Perkins was born in Boston in 1880 and studied at Mount Holyoke College and Columbia University. Moved by the plight of working people, she became a social reformer in New York, and in 1905 she was confirmed in the Episcopal Church, a faith that sustained her work throughout life. In 1933 President Franklin Roosevelt named her Secretary of Labor, making her the first woman in a United States cabinet. For twelve years she helped shape the New Deal, including Social Security, unemployment insurance, the minimum wage and limits on child labor. She later taught at Cornell and died in New York in 1965.

UO-SIN-000742.name: Carthach of Lismore
UO-SIN-000742.life: Carthach, also called Mochuda or Mo Chutu, was an Irish monk of the seventh century, said to have been born in County Kerry. He founded a monastery at Rahan in County Offaly, where hundreds are said to have joined him, and he composed a rule for his monks in Irish verse. Around Easter in the mid-630s he and his community were driven from Rahan, perhaps by a local prince or perhaps over a dispute about the date of Easter. He travelled south to the banks of the Blackwater in County Waterford and founded Lismore, which became a famous school and see. He died there in 637.
UO-SIN-000742.place: Rahan, County Offaly; Lismore, County Waterford

UO-SIN-000743.name: Pachomius of Tabenissi
UO-SIN-000743.life: Pachomius was born around 292 in Upper Egypt to pagan parents and was conscripted into the Roman army as a young man. The kindness of local Christians to the soldiers moved him, and after his discharge he was baptized in about 314. He lived for a time under a hermit, then around 320 founded a community at Tabennisi on the Nile, where monks lived together under a common rule of prayer and manual work. Several more monasteries followed, eventually for both monks and nuns. He is regarded as the father of communal monastic life. He died in the 340s.

UO-SIN-001023.name: Brendan the Navigator
UO-SIN-001023.life: Brendan was born in County Kerry around 484 and became one of the great monastic founders of early Ireland, establishing Clonfert in County Galway about 560 and other communities. He is best remembered for the Voyage of Brendan, a medieval tale written long after his death, in which he and a band of monks sail in a leather boat across the ocean to the Isle of the Blessed, meeting wonders on the way. Scholars regard it as a story of spiritual pilgrimage, though it may reflect real seafaring. The details of his own life are uncertain. He died around 577.

UO-SIN-001024.name: Restituta of Carthage
UO-SIN-001024.life: Restituta was a young Christian woman of North Africa, said to have been put to death for her faith, perhaps in the persecution under Diocletian around 304, though some accounts give an earlier date. Very little is certain about her. A medieval legend says that after being tortured she was set adrift in a burning boat, which an angel guided safely to the island of Ischia, where a woman named Lucina found her dead body on the shore. Devotion to her spread to Italy, perhaps through North African refugees, and a church in Naples and a sanctuary at Lacco Ameno on Ischia bear her name.

UO-SIN-000746.name: John I
UO-SIN-000746.life: John was a native of Tuscany who became bishop of Rome in 523, already old and frail. In 525 the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, an Arian Christian, sent him to Constantinople to ask the emperor Justin to ease his harsh measures against the Arians. John was received with honour, the first pope to visit that city, and obtained part of what Theodoric wanted. Back in Ravenna, however, the king suspected him of siding with the emperor and had him thrown into prison. Weakened by ill treatment, John died there on 18 May 526, and his body was brought to Rome. He is honoured as a martyr.

UO-SIN-000747.name: Dunstan
UO-SIN-000747.life: Dunstan was born near Glastonbury around 909 into a noble Wessex family and was educated by the monks there. He served at court, became a monk and priest, and in 943 was made abbot of Glastonbury, where he restored the Benedictine rule. Exiled to Flanders in 955 after offending King Eadwig, he returned under King Edgar and became archbishop of Canterbury in 959. Together they worked to reform monasteries and strengthen the Church, and Dunstan crowned Edgar at Bath in 973. A skilled musician and metalworker, he became the centre of many folk tales. He died at Canterbury in 988.

UO-SIN-000748.name: Alcuin of York
UO-SIN-000748.life: Alcuin was born in Northumbria around 735 and trained at the cathedral school of York. Meeting the emperor Charlemagne in Italy in 781, he accepted an invitation to the Frankish court and directed its palace school at Aachen, drawing scholars together and raising the standard of learning across the realm. He helped revise the liturgy and the text of the Bible, and wrote hundreds of letters. In 796 he became abbot of St Martin's at Tours, where the clear Carolingian script flourished under his influence. He remained a deacon all his life and died at Tours in 804.

UO-SIN-000249.name: Lydia of Thyatira
UO-SIN-000249.life: Lydia appears in the sixteenth chapter of Acts as a seller of purple cloth, a woman of means from Thyatira in Asia Minor who had settled in the Macedonian city of Philippi. She was a worshipper of God, and one Sabbath, as she joined other women praying beside the river outside the city, she heard Paul speak. The Lord opened her heart. She and her household were baptized, and she urged Paul and his companions to stay at her house. She is regarded as the first known convert to Christianity in Europe, and her home probably became a meeting place for the young church of Philippi.

UO-SIN-001035.name: Julia of Corsica
UO-SIN-001035.life: Julia was a young Christian noblewoman of Carthage who, when the Vandal king Gaiseric captured the city in 439, was sold into slavery to a pagan merchant from Syria named Eusebius. According to the tradition that has come down to us, when his ship put in at northern Corsica he joined a pagan festival, and Julia refused to take part. The governor, Felix, urged her to honour the gods, but she answered that her freedom lay in serving Christ. For this she was tortured and crucified. Monks later rescued her relics, and she is honoured as a patron of Corsica.

UO-SIN-000749.name: Petroc of Cornwall
UO-SIN-000749.life: Petroc was, according to tradition, a Welsh prince, a younger son of King Glywys, who gave up the crown for a life of prayer in the sixth century. He is said to have studied in Ireland and then landed on the River Camel in Cornwall, where he founded a monastery at the place now named Padstow, 'Petroc's Place', and another at Bodmin. Later legends add a tame wolf. His relics came to rest at Bodmin, and his cult spread widely across Cornwall and Devon, so that he is counted among the patrons of Cornwall. He is said to have died about 564.

UO-SIN-001038.name: Vincent of Lérins
UO-SIN-001038.life: Vincent, probably a Gaul from the region of Toul or Toulouse, became a monk on the island of Lérins off the southern coast of France, and was ordained a priest. Around 434, writing under the pen-name Peregrinus, he composed the Commonitory, a short guide for telling true teaching from error. His famous rule held that the faith to hold is what has been believed everywhere, always and by all. He wrote in the shadow of the debate about Augustine's teaching on grace, and some have found him critical of it. He died around 445.

UO-SIN-000751.name: Bede
UO-SIN-000751.life: Bede was born about 673 in Northumbria and spent almost all his life in the monastery of Monkwearmouth and Jarrow. He became a priest at thirty and devoted himself to study, teaching and prayer. He wrote commentaries on Scripture, books on how to reckon time, and, in 731, the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, the chief source for the early English Church. Tradition says he was dictating a translation of John's Gospel as he lay dying in 735. He is the only English-born Doctor of the Church.

UO-SIN-000752.name: Augustine of Canterbury
UO-SIN-000752.life: Augustine was prior of a Benedictine monastery in Rome when Pope Gregory the Great sent him in 596 to bring the gospel to the Anglo-Saxons. With some forty companions he landed in Kent in 597 and was welcomed by King Aethelberht. The king was baptized, and many of his people followed. Augustine made Canterbury his base, founded the cathedral and a monastery, and appointed bishops for London and Rochester. He found it hard to win the cooperation of the older British churches in Wales. He died about 604, and Laurence succeeded him.

UO-SIN-000753.name: Melangell / Monacella
UO-SIN-000753.life: According to legend, Melangell was an Irish princess who fled her father's court to avoid an arranged marriage and came to a remote valley in Powys in Wales, where she lived as a hermit for years. One day, the prince Brochwel, hunting a hare, found her at prayer with the hare hidden in her cloak, and his hounds fled from her. Moved by this, he gave her the valley as a sanctuary, and she founded a community of women there. She is honoured as the patron of hares, which were long called her lambs. Her medieval shrine at Pennant Melangell was rebuilt in modern times.

UO-SIN-000754.name: Mechthild of Magdeburg
UO-SIN-000754.life: Mechthild was born about 1208 into a Saxon noble family and said she received visions from the age of twelve. Around 1230 she went to Magdeburg and lived as a beguine, a woman devoted to prayer and service without belonging to a convent. From about 1250 she wrote The Flowing Light of the Godhead, a book of visions, poems and dialogues, among the first mystical works in German rather than Latin. She also rebuked the failings of the clergy, which drew hostility. In later life, she found shelter among the nuns of Helfta, where she died about 1282, though the date is uncertain.

UO-SIN-000755.name: Maximinus of Trier
UO-SIN-000755.life: Maximinus was born near Poitiers and became bishop of Trier in the 330s, when the city was an imperial residence in the West. A firm defender of the Nicene faith, he welcomed Athanasius of Alexandria when the bishop was exiled and sheltered him for more than two years. When Arian bishops came to the emperor Constans, Maximinus is said to have persuaded him to reject their appeals, and he joined those who urged the council at Sardica in 343. He sent missionaries into the Moselle valley.He died around the middle of the fourth century, and an abbey rose over his tomb at Trier.

UO-SIN-000756.name: Josephine Butler
UO-SIN-000756.life: Josephine Butler was born in Northumberland in 1828 and married the Anglican clergyman George Butler; they later lived in Liverpool, where she grew concerned for poor and exploited women. In 1869 she became the leader of the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts, which subjected women to forced medical examinations, and the Acts were repealed in 1886. She also worked against the trafficking of girls, and with others helped to raise the age of consent from thirteen to sixteen in 1885. Driven by her Christian faith, she wrote widely and died in 1906.

UO-SIN-000758.name: Justin Martyr
UO-SIN-000758.life: Born in Flavia Neapolis, modern Nablus, to a Greek family, Justin searched through the schools of Greek philosophy before an encounter with an old Christian man and the courage of Christians facing death led him to the gospel. He kept his philosopher's cloak and taught Christianity as the true philosophy, opening a school in Rome. His two Apologies defended believers to the emperor, and his Dialogue with Trypho engaged a Jewish scholar over the Scriptures. Denounced under Marcus Aurelius, he was tried by the prefect Rusticus and, with six companions, refused to sacrifice and was beheaded about 165.

UO-SIN-000759.name: Blandina and Her Companions, the Martyrs of Lyons
UO-SIN-000759.life: In the summer of 177, during the reign of Marcus Aurelius, the small Christian community at Lyons in Gaul suffered a savage local persecution. Neighbours shunned them, slaves were tortured into false accusations, and about forty-eight believers died. Among them were the aged bishop Pothinus, who perished in prison, and Sanctus, Maturus, Attalus and the youth Ponticus. The slave woman Blandina, frail in body, endured torment after torment in the arena without wavering, repeating that she was a Christian and did nothing wrong. She died last. Their story survives in a letter from the churches of Lyons and Vienne.

UO-SIN-000760.name: The Martyrs of Uganda
UO-SIN-000760.life: In the kingdom of Buganda, the young king Mwanga II grew suspicious of the growing number of Christian converts at his court, who put loyalty to Christ above his demands. Between 1885 and 1887 some forty-five Anglican and Catholic Christians were put to death. Bishop James Hannington and his companions were killed in 1885. The Catholic Joseph Mukasa was beheaded for rebuking the king. On 3 June 1886 Charles Lwanga and a group of royal pages, including the boy Kizito, were burned alive at Namugongo. Their courage helped the young church to grow across Uganda.

UO-SIN-000761.name: John XXIII
UO-SIN-000761.life: Angelo Roncalli was born in 1881 into a large peasant family at Sotto il Monte, near Bergamo. Ordained in 1904, he served for decades as a Vatican diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey, Greece and France, then became Patriarch of Venice and a cardinal. Elected pope in 1958 at the age of seventy-six, many expected a quiet caretaker. Instead he called the Second Vatican Council, which opened in 1962, and wrote the peace encyclical Pacem in terris. Warm, humorous and approachable, he was widely loved as the Good Pope. He died of cancer on 3 June 1963, before the council ended.

UO-SIN-000762.name: Boniface of Mainz
UO-SIN-000762.life: Born Winfrith in Wessex around 675, Boniface was a monk and teacher at Nursling near Winchester before choosing missionary work on the continent. Pope Gregory II sent him to preach in Germany and gave him the name Boniface. According to tradition, he felled the sacred oak of Thor at Geismar and, when no god struck him down, many were persuaded to turn to Christ. He founded monasteries, including Fulda, organised dioceses and reformed the Frankish church, finally becoming archbishop of Mainz. In 754, preaching in Frisia, he was killed near Dokkum by raiders along with companions. He is called the Apostle of Germany.

UO-SIN-000763.name: Ini Kopuria
UO-SIN-000763.life: Ini Kopuria was born near Maravovo on Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands and rose to be a sergeant in the island constabulary. After an illness and a vision in 1924, he felt called to carry the gospel to those who had not heard it. With Bishop John Steward he founded the Melanesian Brotherhood in 1925, a community of men who vowed poverty, obedience and celibacy for a few years and walked unarmed from village to village. He gave his family land at Tabalia as its home. He left leadership in 1940, married, served as a village deacon, and died in 1945.

UO-SIN-000764.name: Willibald of Eichstatt
UO-SIN-000764.life: Willibald was an English noble from Wessex who, as a boy, was dedicated to monastic life. In 721 he set out on pilgrimage with his father and brother, travelling through Rome and on to the Holy Land, where he visited Nazareth, Bethlehem and Jerusalem; he was probably the first Englishman to do so. After years in Constantinople and a decade at Monte Cassino, he was called by his kinsman Boniface to Germany. Ordained in 741, he became the first bishop of Eichstatt, founded a school there, and with his brother Winnibald built the double monastery at Heidenheim. He died in the 780s.

UO-SIN-000765.name: Melania the Elder
UO-SIN-000765.life: Born about 350 into a wealthy Roman family of Spanish origin, Melania was married young and widowed at twenty-two, having lost her husband and two sons. She gave up her comfortable life and sailed to Egypt, where she supported the monks of Nitria and sheltered exiled clergy. About 380 she settled on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem, founding a convent for women and, with the priest Rufinus, a monastery for men, and welcoming pilgrims for some twenty-seven years. Late in life she returned to Rome to guide her family, including her granddaughter Melania the Younger. She died around 410.

UO-SIN-000766.name: Columba of Iona
UO-SIN-000766.life: Born around 521 in Donegal into a noble Irish family, Columba studied under leading monastic teachers and founded churches and monasteries, among them Derry and Durrow. About 563, perhaps after a bitter quarrel that led to bloodshed, he sailed in a leather-covered boat with twelve companions to Scotland and settled on the island of Iona. From there his community carried the gospel to the Picts and Scots, and Iona became a famous centre of prayer, learning and hospitality. Admired as a scribe, peacemaker and poet, he died before the altar on Iona in 597. His life was written by his successor Adomnan.

UO-SIN-000767.name: Ephrem of Nisibis
UO-SIN-000767.life: Born at Nisibis in Mesopotamia about 306, Ephrem served the church there as a deacon and teacher under its bishops. When Nisibis was handed to Persia in 363, he and many other Christians moved to Edessa, where he taught and wrote until his death in 373. Writing in Syriac, he poured out hymns, sermons and biblical commentaries, using rich imagery to praise God and answer false teaching, and sometimes trained choirs of women to sing them. He is remembered as the Harp of the Spirit. Tradition says he died after caring for victims of plague or famine.

UO-SIN-000768.name: Barnabas the Apostle
UO-SIN-000768.life: Born Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, he sold his land and gave the money to the apostles, who named him Barnabas, meaning son of encouragement. When the church in Jerusalem feared the newly converted Saul, Barnabas vouched for him, and later he brought Paul to Antioch to teach. The two travelled as missionaries to Cyprus and Asia Minor and took part in the council at Jerusalem. After a sharp quarrel over John Mark, Barnabas took Mark back to Cyprus. According to later tradition he was martyred there at Salamis, though the early evidence is thin.

UO-SIN-000769.name: Enmegahbowh
UO-SIN-000769.life: Enmegahbowh, also called John Johnson, was born about 1820 near Rice Lake in what is now Ontario, of Ojibwe and Odawa heritage. He came to Minnesota as a Methodist missionary and later joined the Episcopal Church, working with James Lloyd Breck at Gull Lake and Bishop Henry Whipple. In the 1862 Dakota conflict he risked his life to warn Fort Ripley and helped keep many Ojibwe from joining the fighting. Ordained deacon in 1859 and priest in 1867, he was the first Native American priest of the Episcopal Church. He served his people at White Earth until his death in 1902.

UO-SIN-001074.name: Anthony of Padua
UO-SIN-001074.life: Born in Lisbon in 1195 as Fernando de Bulhoes, he joined the Augustinian canons as a teenager and studied at Coimbra. The sight of the bodies of the first Franciscan martyrs, killed in Morocco, moved him to become a Franciscan about 1220 and take the name Anthony. His learning and powerful preaching soon became known, and Francis himself asked him to teach theology to the friars. He preached across northern Italy and southern France and made Padua his base, where crowds came to hear him. He died there in 1231, aged about thirty-six, and was canonised within a year. He was named a Doctor of the Church in 1946.

UO-SIN-000771.name: Basil of Caesarea
UO-SIN-000771.life: Born about 330 into a devout and wealthy Cappadocian family, Basil studied at Caesarea, Constantinople and Athens, where he befriended Gregory of Nazianzus. Moved by the example of his sister Macrina, he gave himself to the ascetic life and wrote rules for communities that shaped Eastern monasticism. Made bishop of Caesarea in 370, he defended the Nicene faith against Arians and wrote on the Holy Spirit. He was equally known for charity: during famine he fed the hungry and built the Basiliad, a complex of hospice, hospital and poorhouse. He stood up to the emperor Valens, and he died on 1 January 379.

UO-SIN-000772.name: Evelyn Underhill
UO-SIN-000772.life: Born in Wolverhampton in 1875, the only child of a barrister, Evelyn Underhill was a writer who drew thousands of readers to the inner life. Her book Mysticism (1911) made the subject respectable to educated people, and Worship (1936) explored the meaning of the church's prayer. Guided by the Catholic thinker Baron Friedrich von Hugel, she turned to a deeper faith centred on Christ. From 1924 she led retreats and became a well-loved spiritual director and lecturer, one of the first women to address clergy. In her last years she was a committed pacifist. She died in London in June 1941.

UO-SIN-000773.name: Joseph Butler
UO-SIN-000773.life: Born in 1692 at Wantage into a Presbyterian family, Joseph Butler conformed to the Church of England and was ordained in 1718. As preacher at the Rolls Chapel in London he delivered sermons, later published, arguing that human nature is complex and that conscience is our rightful guide, answering Hobbes. In 1736 he published The Analogy of Religion, which met the deists by showing that nature holds the same puzzles as revelation. Chaplain to Queen Caroline, he became bishop of Bristol in 1738, declined Canterbury, and was bishop of Durham from 1750. Quiet and generous, he died at Bath in 1752.

UO-SIN-000774.name: Marina the Monk
UO-SIN-000774.life: According to tradition, Marina was the daughter of a devout man named Eugenios who wished to enter a monastery after his wife died. Rather than be left behind, she cut her hair, dressed as a boy, and entered the monastery with him as Brother Marinos. Accused falsely of fathering a child by an innkeeper's daughter, she accepted the blame in silence, was driven out, and raised the child at the monastery gate. Readmitted years later, she took the hardest tasks. Only at her death was her identity discovered, and the monks begged forgiveness. Sources disagree on her place and date.

UO-SIN-000775.name: Bernard Mizeki
UO-SIN-000775.life: Born about 1861 in Mozambique as Mamiyeri Mitseka, Bernard left home as a boy and found work in Cape Town. He attended night classes run by Anglican missionaries, was baptised in 1886, and showed a gift for languages. In 1891 he went with Bishop Knight-Bruce to Mashonaland, now Zimbabwe, as a catechist, building a mission station at Nhowe near the chief Mangwende and teaching and translating among the Shona. In the 1896 uprising he was warned to flee but would not abandon his converts. On the night of 18 June he was speared outside his hut, and his body was never found.

UO-SIN-000220.name: Adelaide Teague Case
UO-SIN-000220.life: Born in St. Louis in 1887, Adelaide Teague Case studied at Bryn Mawr and took her doctorate at Columbia University. For two decades from 1919 she taught religious education at Teachers College in New York, helping shape it as a modern discipline that respected science and centred on the learner. In 1941 she became Professor of Christian Education at the Episcopal Theological School in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the first woman to hold a full professorship at an Episcopal seminary. A generous teacher and a supporter of women's place in the church, she died in Boston in 1948.

UO-SIN-000776.name: Fillan
UO-SIN-000776.life: Fillan was an Irish monk, probably from Munster, who crossed to Scotland about 717 and is associated with Fife and Perthshire. He is said to have led a monastery in Fife and a hermit's life in a cave at Pittenweem, then lived at Glen Dochart and Strathfillan, where he was buried. According to tradition, a wolf took the place of his slain ox at the plough, and a glow from his arm let him write in the dark. His relics, including a crozier and a bell, were carried by Scots and later associated with Bannockburn. Few reliable details survive, and his dates are uncertain.

UO-SIN-000777.name: Aloysius Gonzaga
UO-SIN-000777.life: Born in 1568 at the castle of Castiglione, Luigi Gonzaga was the eldest son of a marquis and was raised for court and war. He was placed in princely households and met Charles Borromeo, who guided his spiritual life. Despite his father's opposition, he renounced his inheritance in 1585 and joined the Jesuits in Rome. In 1591 plague and famine struck the city, and although his health was frail he nursed the sick in hospitals. He caught the illness himself and died on 21 June, aged twenty-three. He was canonised in 1726 and is honoured as a patron of young people and students.

UO-SIN-000778.name: Alban
UO-SIN-000778.life: Alban is remembered as the first known martyr of Britain. According to Bede, he lived at Verulamium, now St Albans, and was not yet a Christian when he sheltered a priest fleeing persecution. Moved by the man's faith, he was converted, and when soldiers came, he put on the priest's cloak and gave himself up in his place. Refusing to sacrifice to the gods, he was beheaded on a hill outside the town. Tradition adds miracles, such as a river parting for him. The date is uncertain, with 209, 251 and about 304 all proposed. A shrine stood there by the fifth century.

UO-SIN-000779.name: Etheldreda / Audrey of Ely
UO-SIN-000779.life: Born about 636, Etheldreda was a daughter of Anna, king of East Anglia. Married first to a prince named Tondberht, she lived as a virgin; after his death she was given in marriage to Ecgfrith of Northumbria, with Bishop Wilfrid as her counsellor. After years of longing to be a nun, she was allowed to enter the convent at Coldingham, then fled to her own land at Ely, where about 673 she founded a double monastery and ruled as abbess. She died of plague in 679. Her body was said to be found uncorrupted years later, and Ely became a place of pilgrimage.

UO-SIN-000781.name: Moluag of Lismore
UO-SIN-000781.life: Moluag was an Irish monk of the sixth century, a pupil of Comgall at Bangor, who set out with companions to bring the gospel to the Picts of Scotland. About 562 he settled on the island of Lismore in Loch Linnhe, a place long held sacred by the Picts, and made it a centre of prayer and teaching. According to tradition he founded many more communities, including Rosemarkie and Mortlach, which later became bishops' seats. A contemporary of Columba, he is remembered as a missionary bishop of the western Highlands and is said to have died in 592. Reliable records are few.

UO-SIN-000782.name: Isabel Florence Hapgood
UO-SIN-000782.life: Born in Boston in 1851 and raised in Worcester, Massachusetts, Isabel Hapgood had a gift for languages, including Russian and Church Slavonic. She became a leading translator, introducing English readers to Tolstoy, Gogol and Hugo, and worked as a journalist, travelling in Russia in the 1880s. Drawn to the beauty of Orthodox worship, she spent years translating its services; her Service Book of the Holy Orthodox-Catholic Church appeared in 1906 and again in 1922, with the support of Archbishop Tikhon. A lifelong Episcopalian, she never became Orthodox, but her work helped Orthodox and Anglican Christians know one another. She died in New York in 1928.

UO-SIN-001099.name: Cyril of Alexandria
UO-SIN-001099.life: Nephew of the patriarch Theophilus, Cyril became patriarch of Alexandria in 412 and led it until his death in 444. He is remembered chiefly for defending the unity of Christ's person against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, insisting that Mary could rightly be called Theotokos, God-bearer, because the child she bore was truly God. He led the Council of Ephesus in 431, which condemned Nestorius's teaching. His letters and commentaries shaped later doctrine. He was also a forceful, sometimes harsh church politician, and his role in the conflicts of Alexandria remains debated. He was named a Doctor of the Church in 1883.

UO-SIN-000784.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
UO-SIN-000784.life: Born in Asia Minor, probably at Smyrna, Irenaeus as a boy heard the aged bishop Polycarp, who had known the apostle John's circle. He came to Gaul and served as a priest at Lyons; when the persecution of 177 claimed the bishop Pothinus, he succeeded him. His great work Against Heresies answered the Gnostics, who treated the material world as evil, by insisting on one good Creator and on the faith handed down from the apostles. He also urged churches to keep peace over differing customs. He is remembered as a pastor and theologian of unity. He died about 202.

UO-SIN-000785.name: The Apostles Saint Peter and Saint Paul
UO-SIN-000785.life: Peter, a Galilean fisherman, was among the first disciples called by Jesus and became the leading voice of the Twelve, receiving the name Rock. Paul, born Saul at Tarsus, was a Pharisee who persecuted Christians until a vision on the road to Damascus turned him into the apostle to the Gentiles; his letters fill much of the New Testament. They sometimes disagreed, yet both preached the same Lord. According to early tradition, both died at Rome under Nero, Peter by crucifixion and Paul by the sword, about 64 to 67.

UO-SIN-000786.name: The First Martyrs of Rome under Nero
UO-SIN-000786.life: In July of 64 a great fire destroyed much of Rome. Rumour blamed the emperor Nero, and he turned suspicion on the Christians, a small and disliked group. The historian Tacitus records that many were arrested and put to death with cruelty: some were sewn into animal skins and torn by dogs, some were crucified, and others were burned as torches at night in Nero's gardens. Tacitus himself thought them guilty of hatred of humanity, yet noted that the crowd felt pity. These nameless believers were the first Christians killed in Rome. Tradition holds that Peter and Paul died in the same persecution.

UO-SIN-000183.name: Harriet Beecher Stowe
UO-SIN-000183.life: Harriet Beecher Stowe was born in Litchfield, Connecticut, in 1811, the daughter of the preacher Lyman Beecher, and grew up in a household of fervent faith and public conscience. She married Calvin Stowe and raised seven children while writing to supplement the family income. Outraged by the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, she wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin, which appeared in installments and then as a book in 1852. It sold in huge numbers and turned many hearts against slavery. A member of the Episcopal Church in later life, she kept writing until old age and died in Hartford in 1896.

UO-SIN-000002.name: Moses the Black
UO-SIN-000002.life: Moses was an Ethiopian slave in fourth-century Egypt who, after being dismissed by his master, became the fearsome leader of a band of robbers. He was drawn to the desert monks of Scetis, repented, and asked to join them. There he learned humility and patience under the guidance of older monks, was eventually ordained priest, and gathered disciples of his own. He was known for his gentleness toward sinners. According to the tradition, when raiders threatened the monastery around the year 400, he refused to resist, stayed with a few brothers, and was killed, bearing witness to the peace of Christ.

UO-SIN-001106.name: Joshua the Prophet (Son of Nun)
UO-SIN-001106.life: Joshua, son of Nun, appears in the Bible as the faithful servant of Moses. He led Israel's first battle after the Exodus, accompanied Moses up Sinai, and as one of the twelve spies urged trust in God's promise with Caleb. After Moses died, he led the people across the Jordan into Canaan, where the fall of Jericho is the best-remembered event. At Shechem, near the end of his life, he called the tribes to choose whom they would serve, declaring that he and his house would serve the Lord. He died aged one hundred and ten and was buried in the hill country of Ephraim.
UO-SIN-001106.period: died, as told in the Book of Joshua, aged 110

UO-SIN-000188.name: Elizabeth of Portugal
UO-SIN-000188.life: Born in 1271, Elizabeth was an Aragonese princess given in marriage to King Denis of Portugal, whose faithfulness to her was poor. She answered with patience, prayer, and generosity, caring for the sick, the poor, and pilgrims and founding charitable houses. Her gift for reconciliation became famous. In 1323 she is said to have ridden between the armies of her husband and her rebel son Afonso to stop a battle. Widowed in 1325, she lived near a Poor Clare convent at Coimbra. She died at Estremoz in 1336 while travelling to make peace between her son and the king of Castile.

UO-SIN-000005.name: Palladius
UO-SIN-000005.life: Palladius came from a distinguished family in Gaul and served as a deacon before Pope Celestine I consecrated him bishop in 431 and sent him to the Christians of Ireland, 'the Scots believing in Christ'. According to Irish tradition he landed in what is now County Wicklow, founded a few churches, and met hostility from a local ruler. His mission was short. Later Scottish tradition says he went on to northern Britain and was buried there, though historians treat those accounts with caution. His story was partly confused with that of Patrick, who carried the work of the Irish mission much further.

UO-SIN-000006.name: Eva Lee Matthews
UO-SIN-000006.life: Eva Lee Matthews was born in 1862 into a prominent family in Glendale, Ohio, her father being a Supreme Court justice. Drawn to the religious life at a time when Episcopal convents were still few, she and Beatrice Henderson founded the Community of the Transfiguration in 1898, and she became Mother Eva Mary. The sisters worked with mothers and children near Cincinnati, ran schools, and cared for the poor, and later sent missionaries to China. She sought to join prayer and service, in the manner of Mary and Martha. She died on 6 July 1928.

UO-SIN-000007.name: Boisil
UO-SIN-000007.life: Boisil was a seventh-century monk of the young monastery of Melrose in the Scottish borders, serving as prior under Abbot Eata. He is best remembered as the teacher of Cuthbert, who came to Melrose as a young man in 651. Boisil is said to have recognised his promise at once and taught him the Scriptures. He was also known for care of the sick. Bede tells that he foresaw both a coming plague and Cuthbert's future as a bishop. Boisil died in the plague, around 664, and the Scottish village of St Boswells still bears his name.

UO-SIN-000008.name: Priscilla and Aquila
UO-SIN-000008.life: Priscilla and Aquila were a Jewish Christian married couple of the first century, tentmakers by trade. Expelled from Rome under the emperor Claudius, they settled in Corinth, where they welcomed Paul into their home and workshop. They later moved to Ephesus and hosted a church in their house. When the learned preacher Apollos spoke boldly but knew only part of the faith, they took him aside and explained the way of God more fully. Paul spoke of them as fellow workers who risked their necks for him. Priscilla is often named first, suggesting her prominence.

UO-SIN-000009.name: Augustine Zhao Rong and the Martyrs of China
UO-SIN-000009.life: These are 120 Catholics, Chinese and foreign, who died for their faith in China between 1648 and 1930, canonized together in 2000. Many were killed in the Boxer uprising of 1900, including lay people, catechists, and children. Among the earlier martyrs was Francisco de Capillas, beheaded in 1648, and Bishop Gabriel Dufresse, executed in 1815. Augustine Zhao Rong, born in Guizhou in 1746, was a soldier who guarded Christian prisoners, was moved by their faith, and was baptized. He became one of the first Chinese diocesan priests and died from beatings in prison in 1815.

UO-SIN-000010.name: Anthony and Theodosius of the Kyiv Caves
UO-SIN-000010.life: Anthony and Theodosius founded the Monastery of the Caves above the Dnipro at Kyiv in the eleventh century. Anthony, born near Chernihiv, lived as a monk on Mount Athos and returned to Rus' to live as a hermit in a cave, eating little and praying much. Disciples gathered around him. Theodosius, born around 1009, became abbot and introduced the communal rule of the Studite monasteries, with shared work, prayer, and meals. Under him the community grew into the great centre of monastic life, learning, and charity in Rus'. Anthony died around 1073 and Theodosius in 1074.

UO-SIN-000011.name: Benedict of Nursia
UO-SIN-000011.life: Born in Nursia in Italy around 480, Benedict left his studies in Rome to seek God in solitude, living in a cave near Subiaco. Disciples followed him, and he founded several small communities before settling at Monte Cassino around 530. There he wrote his Rule, a short guide for monks seeking God together through prayer, work, humility, and obedience, and marked by moderation. Most of what is known of him comes from Pope Gregory the Great's Dialogues, whose details historians debate. He died around 547, and his Rule became the foundation of Western monasticism.

UO-SIN-000203.name: Veronica
UO-SIN-000203.life: Veronica does not appear in the Gospels. According to a medieval tradition, a woman of Jerusalem was moved by pity when Jesus carried his cross to Calvary and offered him her veil to wipe his face; when it was returned, his features were found imprinted on the cloth. Her name probably arose from the Latin vera icon, 'true image', the title of the relic itself. Eastern traditions identify her with Berenice, and some with the woman healed of a long haemorrhage. Whatever its origin, her act of compassion became the sixth Station of the Cross.

UO-SIN-000013.name: Henry
UO-SIN-000013.life: According to tradition, Henry was an Englishman who became bishop of Uppsala in Sweden and accompanied King Eric IX on a crusade to Finland in the 1150s. He stayed to organise the new Christian community and was murdered, it is said, by a Finnish farmer he had disciplined. Folk tales name the killer Lalli and place the death on the ice of Lake Koylio. Historians note that there are no contemporary records of him, and his earliest life was written long afterwards. Whatever the facts, Henry has long been honoured as the patron of Finland, remembered as its first bishop and martyr.

UO-SIN-000014.name: Argula von Grumbach
UO-SIN-000014.life: Argula von Stauff was born in Bavaria in 1492 and, unusually for a girl, was given a Bible in German. She married Friedrich von Grumbach and came to embrace Luther's teaching. In 1523, when the University of Ingolstadt arrested a young Lutheran student, Arsacius Seehofer, she wrote an open letter to the faculty, backing her arguments with some eighty scriptural references. It was printed and widely read. Her bold stand cost her dearly: her husband lost his post and she faced ridicule. She continued to write and to correspond with reformers, and died around 1554.

UO-SIN-000210.name: Vladimir of Kyiv
UO-SIN-000210.life: Vladimir, born around 958, became grand prince of Kyiv in 978 and began as a pagan ruler with many wives and temples to the old gods. Around 988 he was baptized, and he married Anna, sister of the Byzantine emperor. He then ordered the idols of Kyiv cast down and the people baptized in the Dnipro, and built the Church of the Tithes. He is remembered for charity to the poor and for bringing Byzantine Christianity to the Rus' lands, shaping the faith of Ukraine, Russia, and Belarus. He died in 1015.

UO-SIN-000016.name: Osmund of Salisbury
UO-SIN-000016.life: Osmund was a Norman nobleman who came to England in the time of William the Conqueror and served him as chancellor. Around 1078 he became bishop of Salisbury. He built a new cathedral at Old Sarum, consecrated in 1092, and gave it a chapter of canons with defined offices. He also arranged the ordering of services for his diocese; this became the Sarum Use, which spread widely across the British Isles. He was learned and austere, and is said to have copied books himself. He died in 1099 and was formally canonized in 1457.

UO-SIN-000017.name: William White
UO-SIN-000017.life: William White was born in Philadelphia in 1748 and was ordained in England. When the Revolution came, he took the patriot side and served as chaplain to the Continental Congress while leading Christ Church. After the war, he proposed in a pamphlet that the Episcopal churches organise themselves without waiting for bishops from England. He helped shape the new church's constitution, including a place for laypeople in its governance. Consecrated bishop of Pennsylvania in London in 1787, he served as Presiding Bishop and led his diocese for almost fifty years, also founding schools and charities. He died in 1836.

UO-SIN-000217.name: Elizabeth Ferard
UO-SIN-000217.life: Elizabeth Ferard was born in 1825 into a Huguenot-descended family in London. After her mother's death she felt called to serve, and visited the Lutheran deaconess community at Kaiserswerth in Germany. With the encouragement of Archibald Tait, bishop of London, she founded the North London Deaconess Institution in 1861. On 18 July 1862 she was set apart by the bishop as the first deaconess of the Church of England. She and her companions nursed the sick, taught, and visited the poor in London parishes. Poor health later forced her to step down. She died in 1883, and her work lives on in the Community of St Andrew.

UO-SIN-000019.name: Macrina of Caesarea
UO-SIN-000019.life: Macrina was born around 327 in Cappadocia, the eldest of a large and devout family that included Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa. After the death of the man she was to marry, she chose a life of prayer. She helped to educate her younger brothers and turned the family estate in Pontus into a household community where women of every background lived as equals. Gregory, who wrote her life, describes her as his teacher in faith, and gives her the leading voice in his dialogue on the soul. She died in 379, with prayers on her lips.

UO-SIN-000020.name: Elijah the Prophet
UO-SIN-000020.life: Elijah was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century BC, in the days of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel. He called the people back to the God of Israel, most famously on Mount Carmel, where he challenged the prophets of Baal. Fleeing Jezebel, he met God at Horeb not in wind or fire but in a still, small voice. He called Elisha to follow him, and was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind. Later generations expected his return, and the New Testament links him with John the Baptist and with Jesus at the Transfiguration.

UO-SIN-000021.name: Maria Skobtsova
UO-SIN-000021.life: Born Elizaveta Pilenko in Riga in 1891, she was a poet and political activist who fled revolutionary Russia and settled in Paris. After personal tragedies and a deepening faith, she took monastic vows in 1932 as Mother Maria, and she insisted that service to the neighbour was the heart of monastic life. She opened a hostel on Rue de Lourmel for the poor and homeless. During the German occupation she sheltered Jews, for which she was arrested in 1943 and sent to Ravensbruck, where she died on 31 March 1945. Her son Yuri and chaplain Fr Dimitri also died in captivity.

UO-SIN-000022.name: Mary Magdalene
UO-SIN-000022.life: Mary of Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee, followed Jesus after he freed her from seven demons, and she helped to support his ministry. She stood at the cross, saw where he was laid, and on Easter morning came to the tomb. In John's Gospel she meets the risen Lord and is sent to tell the disciples, which is why she is called the apostle to the apostles. A later Western tradition wrongly identified her with a repentant sinner and with Mary of Bethany; the Gospels say nothing of this. Other traditions have her ending her life at Ephesus or in Provence.

UO-SIN-000023.name: John Cassian
UO-SIN-000023.life: John Cassian was born around 360, probably in the Balkans, and travelled with his friend Germanus to Bethlehem and then to the desert monks of Egypt, whose lives he studied for some fifteen years. He later became a deacon in Constantinople under John Chrysostom and carried his cause to Rome. Around 415 he settled at Marseille and founded monasteries for men and women. There he wrote the Institutes and the Conferences, recording the teachings of the desert fathers on prayer and the struggle with vice. Benedict commended them to his monks. Cassian died around 435.

UO-SIN-000024.name: Thomas à Kempis
UO-SIN-000024.life: Thomas was born around 1380 in Kempen, near Cologne, and was educated at Deventer among the Brethren of the Common Life, whose simple, inward devotion shaped him. In 1406 he entered the Augustinian monastery of Mount St Agnes near Zwolle, where he was ordained priest in 1413 and spent the rest of his life copying manuscripts, writing, and guiding novices. His best-known work is The Imitation of Christ, written for those novices and still widely read, which calls the reader to humility, inner peace, and love of Christ. He died in 1471.

UO-SIN-000025.name: James the Apostle
UO-SIN-000025.life: James, son of Zebedee, was a Galilean fisherman who left his boat and his father to follow Jesus, with his brother John. Jesus nicknamed the brothers Sons of Thunder. James was one of the three closest to Jesus, present at the raising of Jairus's daughter, the Transfiguration, and Gethsemane. He was put to death by the sword under Herod Agrippa around the year 44, the first of the apostles to die for the faith. A later tradition holds that his body was taken to Galicia, and his shrine at Santiago de Compostela became a great goal of pilgrimage.
UO-SIN-000025.place: Galilee; Jerusalem; Santiago de Compostela by tradition

UO-SIN-000026.name: Joachim and Anne
UO-SIN-000026.life: The Gospels do not name the parents of Mary; their names come from an early second-century writing, the Protevangelium of James. According to that account, Joachim was a devout and generous man, and Anne his wife, and they grew old without children. Joachim withdrew into the desert to fast and pray, and angels told them both that they would have a child. Their daughter Mary was dedicated to God. The story is a tradition rather than history, but it has inspired devotion for centuries, and the two are honoured as the grandparents of Jesus and patrons of grandparents.

UO-SIN-000027.name: William Reed Huntington
UO-SIN-000027.life: William Reed Huntington was born in Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1838, graduated from Harvard, and was ordained in the Episcopal Church in 1861 to 1862. He served as rector of All Saints, Worcester, and from 1883 until his death of Grace Church in New York. In 1870 he proposed four essentials of church unity: Scripture, the creeds, the two sacraments, and the historic episcopate. This became the Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral, adopted by the American bishops in 1886 and the Lambeth Conference in 1888. He was also the leading voice in the Prayer Book revision of 1892. He died in 1909.

UO-SIN-000028.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
UO-SIN-000028.life: Bach was born in Eisenach in 1685 into a family of musicians and served as organist and court musician before becoming, in 1723, cantor of the St Thomas School at Leipzig, where he provided music for the city's churches until his death. A devout Lutheran, he wrote hundreds of cantatas, the Passions, the Mass in B minor, and organ and keyboard works that explore the possibilities of counterpoint. He is said to have dedicated his work to the glory of God alone. Little known beyond Germany in his lifetime, he died in Leipzig in 1750 and is now counted among the greatest of composers.

UO-SIN-000029.name: Mary, Martha, and Lazarus
UO-SIN-000029.life: Mary, Martha, and their brother Lazarus lived at Bethany near Jerusalem, and the Gospels say Jesus loved them. In Luke, Martha is busy with hospitality while Mary sits at Jesus' feet to listen, and Jesus says Mary has chosen the better part. In John, Lazarus falls ill and dies; Martha goes to meet Jesus and confesses him as the Christ, and Jesus calls Lazarus from the tomb. Mary later anoints Jesus' feet. Later legends carry them to Cyprus or Provence, but nothing certain is known of their lives after the Gospels.

UO-SIN-000030.name: William Wilberforce
UO-SIN-000030.life: Wilberforce was born in Hull in 1759 and entered Parliament in 1780. Around 1785 he experienced an evangelical conversion that redirected his life toward moral reform. Working with friends of the Clapham circle, among them Thomas Clarkson and Granville Sharp, he led the parliamentary campaign against the slave trade for twenty years until it was abolished in 1807. He also supported missions, education, and the relief of the poor. He lived to hear that Parliament had passed the Slavery Abolition Act in 1833, and died three days later. He is buried in Westminster Abbey.

UO-SIN-000031.name: Ignatius of Loyola
UO-SIN-000031.life: Born in 1491 into a Basque noble family, Ignatius was a soldier until a cannonball broke his leg at Pamplona in 1521. While recovering he read about Christ and the saints, and his heart turned. At Manresa he prayed and fasted for nearly a year and began to write the Spiritual Exercises, a guided retreat for discerning God's will. He studied in Paris, gathered companions, and in 1540 won papal approval for the Society of Jesus, whose members served in teaching, preaching, and mission. He guided the order from Rome until his death in 1556.

UO-SIN-000093.name: Thérèse of Lisieux
UO-SIN-000093.life: Born in Alençon in 1873, Thérèse Martin lost her mother at four and grew up in Lisieux in Normandy. At fifteen she won permission to enter the Carmelite convent there, where she lived hidden and ordinary days among her sisters, three of them her own. She taught what she called her little way: doing small things with great love and trusting God like a child. Tuberculosis took her life at twenty-four, in 1897. Her memoir, Story of a Soul, carried her gentle spirituality around the world. She was canonized in 1925 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1997.

UO-SIN-000094.name: Remigius of Rheims
UO-SIN-000094.life: Remigius was born around 437 into a Gallo-Roman family and, admired for his learning and eloquence, was made bishop of Reims while still very young, at about twenty-two. He is remembered above all for his dealings with Clovis, king of the Franks. After Clovis's victory over the Alemanni, Remigius baptized him at Reims, around 496, together with many of his warriors; later accounts speak of three thousand. With royal support he founded churches and sees across northern Gaul. He served as bishop for some seventy years and died about 533, honored as the apostle of the Franks.

UO-SIN-000095.name: John Raleigh Mott
UO-SIN-000095.life: Born in 1865 in New York and raised in Iowa, John Mott was a Methodist layman who gave his life to drawing Christians together for mission. A Cornell graduate, he served as student secretary of the YMCA, helped found the World Student Christian Federation in 1895, and travelled the world organizing student movements. He presided over the great Edinburgh missionary conference of 1910, a landmark of the modern ecumenical movement, and helped shape the World Council of Churches. In 1946 he shared the Nobel Peace Prize. He died in Florida in 1955 at eighty-nine.

UO-SIN-000096.name: Francis of Assisi
UO-SIN-000096.life: Giovanni di Bernardone was born around 1181 in Assisi, the son of a wealthy cloth merchant, and spent his youth in comfort and song. War, captivity and illness turned him toward God; before the crucifix at San Damiano he heard a call to rebuild the Church. He renounced his inheritance, embraced poverty, and gathered companions who became the Friars Minor, approved in 1210. With Clare he began the Poor Clares. He loved creation and preached to all creatures. In 1224 he is said to have received the wounds of Christ. He died in 1226 and was canonized two years later.

UO-SIN-000097.name: Faustina Kowalska
UO-SIN-000097.life: Helena Kowalska was born in 1905 to a poor peasant family in Głogowiec, Poland, the third of ten children. She worked as a housekeeper while longing for convent life, and in 1925 she entered the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy, taking the name Maria Faustina. She served as cook, gardener and porter in Kraków, Płock and Vilnius. She reported visions of Christ and recorded them in a Diary, from which the devotion to Divine Mercy grew, including the image signed Jesus, I trust in You. She died of tuberculosis in Kraków in 1938, aged thirty-three, and was canonized in 2000.

UO-SIN-000407.name: Bruno of Cologne
UO-SIN-000407.life: Born around 1030 in Cologne, Bruno studied and then taught at Reims, where he headed the cathedral school for many years; his pupils included the future Pope Urban II. He declined the offer of the archbishopric and chose instead to leave the world. In 1084, with six companions, he settled in the wild mountains of the Chartreuse near Grenoble, where they lived in separate cells in silence and prayer. This became the Carthusian order. Called to Rome by Urban, he later withdrew to Calabria in southern Italy and founded a second community there. He died in 1101.

UO-SIN-000099.name: Birgitta of Sweden
UO-SIN-000099.life: Born around 1303 into a noble Swedish family, Birgitta married at thirteen and raised eight children, among them Catherine, later a saint. She served at the royal court and made the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela. After her husband died in 1344 she gave herself to prayer and penance and began to record visions, later gathered as her Revelations. She founded the Bridgettine order at Vadstena, then moved to Rome in 1350, where she cared for the poor and urged reform of the Church and the pope's return from Avignon. She died there in 1373 and was canonized in 1391.

UO-SIN-000100.name: Alexander Penrose Forbes
UO-SIN-000100.life: Born in Edinburgh in 1817, Alexander Forbes began a career in India before illness brought him home and then to Oxford, where the Oxford Movement shaped his faith. Ordained in 1844, he became Bishop of Brechin in 1847 and made Dundee his base, serving as pastor of St Paul's and encouraging the building of several churches. His 1857 charge on the Eucharist, upholding the real presence, led to a trial and a mild censure in 1860, though he never wavered. A learned writer on the Creed and the Articles, he died in Dundee in 1875.

UO-SIN-000101.name: Robert Grosseteste
UO-SIN-000101.life: Born of humble family in Suffolk around 1170, Robert Grosseteste studied at Oxford and became one of the great scholars of his age. He lectured in theology to the Franciscans there, studied light and optics, and translated Greek works into Latin. In 1235 he became Bishop of Lincoln, a vast diocese. He visited its parishes tirelessly, rebuked negligent clergy, and stood up to both king and pope when he believed the Church's duty to souls was at stake. His insistence that the care of souls comes first marked his whole episcopate. He died at Buckden in October 1253.

UO-SIN-000102.name: Vida Dutton Scudder
UO-SIN-000102.life: Vida Scudder was born in 1861 in Madurai, India, to missionary parents, and was raised in Massachusetts by her widowed mother. After Smith College and Oxford she taught English literature at Wellesley for four decades. Her Christian faith led her to the poor: she helped found Denison House, a Boston settlement, joined the Companions of the Holy Cross, and became a Christian socialist who supported striking workers in Lawrence in 1912. She wrote many books on literature, social reform and Franciscan history, and her autobiography, On Journey. She died in Wellesley in 1954, aged ninety-two.

UO-SIN-000103.name: Philip
UO-SIN-000103.life: Philip was one of the Seven chosen in Jerusalem to oversee the care of widows in the earliest church. When persecution scattered the believers, he preached in Samaria with great success. Led by an angel along the road from Jerusalem to Gaza, he met an Ethiopian court official reading Isaiah, explained the passage in light of Jesus, and baptized him. Later he settled in Caesarea, where he welcomed Paul, and had four daughters who prophesied. He is called the Evangelist. Later tradition says he became a bishop in Asia Minor, but the New Testament tells us nothing of his death.

UO-SIN-000104.name: Edith Cavell
UO-SIN-000104.life: Born in 1865 in the Norfolk village of Swardeston, Edith Cavell trained as a nurse in London and in 1907 became matron of a pioneering nursing school in Brussels. When Germany occupied Belgium in 1914 she sheltered wounded British and French soldiers and helped some two hundred escape to the neutral Netherlands. Arrested in August 1915, she admitted what she had done and was sentenced to death. On the eve of her execution she said that patriotism is not enough and that she must have no hatred or bitterness toward anyone. She was shot at dawn on 12 October 1915.

UO-SIN-000105.name: Edward the Confessor
UO-SIN-000105.life: Born around 1003, Edward was the son of King Æthelred and Emma of Normandy, and spent some twenty-five years in exile in Normandy while the Danes ruled England. He was crowned in 1043 and reigned for twenty-four years, a time of comparative peace, during which he relieved his people of heavy taxation. He was known for his piety and generosity to the poor. His great work was the rebuilding of Westminster Abbey, dedicated a week before his death on 5 January 1066, and where he was buried. He left no heir, and his death led to the Norman Conquest. He was canonized in 1161.

UO-SIN-000106.name: Samuel Isaac Joseph Schereschewsky
UO-SIN-000106.life: Born in 1831 in Lithuania to a Jewish family, Schereschewsky was trained for the rabbinate but found faith in Christ through a Hebrew New Testament. He emigrated to America, was baptized, and became an Episcopal priest, sailing to China in 1859. Elected missionary bishop of Shanghai in 1877, he founded St John's College, which grew into a university. A sunstroke in 1881 left him largely paralyzed, and he resigned the see, yet for more than twenty years he went on translating, typing with a single finger. His Bibles in Mandarin and classical Chinese served countless readers. He died in Tokyo in 1906.

UO-SIN-000107.name: Teresa of Avila
UO-SIN-000107.life: Born in Ávila, Spain, in 1515, Teresa entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation as a young woman and lived there for years amid lax observance, while growing in deep prayer. In 1562 she founded the small reformed convent of San José, stressing poverty, silence and contemplation. Working with John of the Cross, she spread the reform of the Discalced Carmelites, founding some seventeen convents despite opposition and ill health. Her books, including The Way of Perfection and The Interior Castle, are classics on prayer. She died at Alba de Tormes in 1582, was canonized in 1622, and in 1970 became the first woman named a Doctor of the Church.

UO-SIN-000108.name: Hugh Latimer, Nicholas Ridley and Thomas Cranmer
UO-SIN-000108.life: These three leaders of the English Reformation were burned under Queen Mary I. Hugh Latimer, a Cambridge scholar turned fiery preacher, became Bishop of Worcester. Nicholas Ridley, Bishop of Rochester and then London, helped Cranmer shape the Book of Common Prayer. Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1533, gave the English church its liturgy. Latimer and Ridley died together at Oxford on 16 October 1555; Latimer reportedly urged his friend to be of good courage, for they would light a candle in England that would never be put out. Cranmer, after recanting under pressure, withdrew his recantations and was burned on 21 March 1556.

UO-SIN-000109.name: Ignatius of Antioch
UO-SIN-000109.life: Ignatius was an early bishop of Antioch in Syria, taking the name Theophoros, God-bearer. Condemned for his faith under the emperor Trajan, he was taken under guard to Rome to face the beasts in the arena. On the way he wrote seven letters, to churches in Asia Minor, to Rome and to Bishop Polycarp, urging unity around the bishop, warning against false teaching, and praising the Eucharist as the medicine of immortality. He begged the Romans not to save him from martyrdom. Tradition places his death around 108 under Trajan, though scholars debate the date, which may lie between about 108 and 140.

UO-SIN-000110.name: Saint Luke the Evangelist
UO-SIN-000110.life: Luke is traditionally held to have been a Gentile physician from Antioch in Syria and a companion of Paul on his journeys, the beloved physician of Paul's letters. Tradition names him as author of the Gospel that bears his name and of the Acts of the Apostles, which together make up a large part of the New Testament. His Gospel, written with notable literary care, stresses mercy, the poor, women and the outcast. Later tradition says he died at about eighty-four in Greece, and that he was the first to paint icons of Mary. He is honored as patron of physicians and artists.

UO-SIN-000111.name: Henry Martyn
UO-SIN-000111.life: Born in Truro, Cornwall, in 1781, Henry Martyn was a brilliant Cambridge mathematician who, under the influence of Charles Simeon, turned from law to the ministry. He sailed for India in 1805 as a chaplain of the East India Company, and devoted himself to languages. He translated the New Testament into Urdu and Persian and helped provide the Book of Common Prayer in Urdu. In 1811 he travelled to Persia to revise his Persian translation and present it to the Shah. On the journey home, worn out with fever, he died at Tokat in Turkey in October 1812, aged only thirty-one.

UO-SIN-000112.name: Cornelius the Centurion
UO-SIN-000112.life: Cornelius was a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea in the first century, described in Acts as a devout man who feared God, gave generously to the poor, and prayed constantly. An angel directed him to send for Peter, who had meanwhile received a vision teaching that God shows no partiality. When Peter preached in Cornelius's house, the Holy Spirit fell on all who listened, and Peter had them baptized. This opened the Church to Gentiles without circumcision, a decision later confirmed at Jerusalem. Later traditions make Cornelius a bishop, either of Caesarea or of Scepsis in Asia Minor, but this cannot be verified.

UO-SIN-000113.name: Hilarion
UO-SIN-000113.life: Hilarion was born around 291 near Gaza to pagan parents, studied in Alexandria, and there became a Christian. He visited the great hermit Anthony in Egypt, then returned to Palestine and lived as a hermit in the wilderness near Gaza, weaving baskets and fasting. His reputation drew disciples, and he is regarded as the founder of monasticism in Palestine. According to Jerome, who wrote his life around 391 and may have exaggerated his deeds, many were healed through him. Seeking solitude, he travelled through Egypt, Sicily and Dalmatia and finally settled in Cyprus, where he died in 371, aged about eighty.

UO-SIN-000459.name: Donatus of Fiesole
UO-SIN-000459.life: Born in Ireland of a noble family, Donatus was a scholar and teacher who travelled to Rome as a pilgrim about 816. According to tradition, on his return journey he came to Fiesole in Tuscany just as the people were praying for a new bishop; when he entered the cathedral the bells rang and the candles lit of themselves, and he was chosen. He served as bishop from about 829 until 876, restoring church life and learning, advising the Carolingian rulers Lothair and Louis II, and teaching grammar and poetry. He wrote a life of Saint Brigid and his own epitaph, which mentions his Irish birth.

UO-SIN-000115.name: Saint James of Jerusalem
UO-SIN-000115.life: James, called the Just and the brother of the Lord, led the Jerusalem church in its earliest decades. Paul counts him among the pillars of the Church with Peter and John. At the Council of Jerusalem, around 50, he spoke decisively in favor of welcoming Gentile converts without requiring circumcision. He was known as a man of prayer. The historian Josephus reports that he was put to death by stoning around 62 at the instigation of the high priest; another early tradition says he was thrown from the Temple. How he was related to Jesus is variously understood.

UO-SIN-000116.name: Hiram Hisanori Kano
UO-SIN-000116.life: Born in 1889 into a Japanese noble family, Hiram Kano studied agriculture in Japan and Nebraska, farmed sugar beets, and taught English to Japanese immigrants in the Great Plains. Ordained deacon in 1928 and priest in 1936, he founded Episcopal congregations at Mitchell and North Platte. Within hours of Pearl Harbor he was arrested as a suspected danger, and was held in several internment camps for about three years, separated from his family. There he taught, led worship and ministered to fellow internees, guards and prisoners of war. Released in 1944, he studied at Nashotah House, then served Nebraska's Japanese residents until 1957. He died in 1988.

UO-SIN-000117.name: Tabitha (Dorcas) of Joppa
UO-SIN-000117.life: Tabitha, called Dorcas in Greek, a name meaning gazelle, lived in the coastal town of Joppa. The Acts of the Apostles calls her a disciple, the only woman given that title there, and says she was full of good works and acts of charity. When she fell ill and died, her friends washed her body and sent for Peter, who was nearby at Lydda. In the upper room the widows stood weeping, showing the coats and garments she had made for them. Peter knelt and prayed, then told her to rise, and she opened her eyes and sat up. The news led many in Joppa to believe.

UO-SIN-000118.name: Alfred the Great
UO-SIN-000118.life: Born about 849, the youngest son of King Æthelwulf, Alfred became king of Wessex in 871 when Viking armies threatened to overrun England. After years of hard fighting, even hiding in the Somerset marshes, he won a decisive victory at Edington in 878 and made peace with the Danish leader Guthrum, who accepted baptism. He built fortified towns, strengthened his army and ships, and issued a code of laws that protected the weak. Valuing learning, he gathered scholars, learned Latin himself, and had important Christian works translated into English. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle was begun in his reign. He died on 26 October 899.

UO-SIN-000119.name: Odran of Iona
UO-SIN-000119.life: According to tradition, Odran was an Irish monk, abbot of Tyfarnham and founder of Latteragh, who was one of twelve companions sailing with Columba to Iona in Scotland. Tradition says he was the first of the community to die there, foretelling it himself, and Columba promised that anyone praying at his grave must also ask Odran's prayers. Iona's burial ground grew around his resting place. A later folk legend says he volunteered to be buried alive beneath the walls of the chapel to make them stand, but this is almost certainly a story and not history. The dates are uncertain, and sources give both 548 and about 563.

UO-SIN-000120.name: Saint Simon and Saint Jude
UO-SIN-000120.life: Simon the Zealot and Jude, also called Thaddaeus, were two of the Twelve Apostles. The Gospels name them but record almost nothing else of them, and Jude is not to be confused with Judas Iscariot. A letter in the New Testament bears Jude's name. Later tradition, much of it legendary, says that Simon preached in Egypt and then joined Jude in Persia, where both were martyred; Simon is said to have been sawn in two, though one early writer says he died peacefully at Edessa. In art Simon carries a saw and Jude a club or an image of Christ. Jude is also called the patron of desperate causes.

UO-SIN-000121.name: James Hannington and his Companions
UO-SIN-000121.life: James Hannington, born in Sussex in 1847, was ordained in 1874 and offered himself to the Church Missionary Society for East Africa. Illness cut short his first journey in 1882-83. Consecrated in 1884 as the first bishop of Eastern Equatorial Africa, he set out in 1885 to find a shorter route to Buganda through Busoga. King Mwanga, fearing that approach from the east meant foreign invasion, had him seized, and Hannington and most of his African porters were put to death on 29 October 1885. His companions were the Africans who traveled and died with him.

UO-SIN-000122.name: Maryam of Qidun
UO-SIN-000122.life: Maryam, also called Mary the Harlot, is a popular Syriac saint of the fourth century. According to tradition, she was orphaned young and raised by her uncle, the hermit Abraham of Qidun near Edessa, in a cell beside his own. At about twenty she was deceived by a false monk and, overcome with shame, fled and fell into a life of sin in a distant town. Abraham, disguised as a customer, found her and brought her home with tenderness instead of reproach. She spent the rest of her life in repentance and prayer, remembered as a sign of God's mercy.

UO-SIN-000123.name: Paul Shinji Sasaki and Philip Lindel Tsen
UO-SIN-000123.life: Paul Sasaki and Philip Tsen were Asian Anglican bishops who led their churches through war. Sasaki, born in 1885, became the first Japanese diocesan bishop, of Mid-Japan, in 1935, and later Bishop of Tokyo. In 1942 he resisted government pressure to fold his church into a state-sponsored union of Protestants, and he was imprisoned and ill-treated in 1944-45. He died in 1946. Tsen, born in 1885 into poverty in Wuhu, China, and taken in by an American mission, became Bishop of Honan and the first Chinese Presiding Bishop of his church. He served his people through war, endured house arrest after 1948, and died in 1954.

UO-SIN-000154.name: Charles de Foucauld
UO-SIN-000154.life: Born in Strasbourg in 1858 and orphaned young, Charles de Foucauld became a French cavalry officer, then an explorer of Morocco, and drifted from the faith of his childhood. In 1886, guided by his cousin and a Paris priest, he returned to Christ and set out on a search that led him to the Holy Land and the Trappists. Ordained in 1901, he settled in the Algerian Sahara, first at Béni Abbès and then among the Tuareg at Tamanrasset. There he offered hospitality, spoke against slavery, and compiled a Tuareg-French dictionary. Raiders shot him at his hermitage on 1 December 1916.

UO-SIN-000155.name: Channing Moore Williams
UO-SIN-000155.life: A Richmond, Virginia, farmer's son, Channing Moore Williams trained at Virginia Theological Seminary and sailed for China, where he was ordained priest. In 1859 he became one of the first Episcopal missionaries to Japan, landing at Nagasaki. Consecrated bishop in 1866 with oversight of both countries, he turned his energy to Japan once it opened to the West, moving to Tokyo in 1874. There he founded the school that became Rikkyo University, translated parts of the Prayer Book, and helped unite the mission churches into the Nippon Sei Ko Kai. He worked in Japan until 1908 and died in Richmond in 1910.
UO-SIN-000155.place: Richmond, Virginia; Nagasaki and Tokyo, Japan

UO-SIN-000156.name: Francis Xavier
UO-SIN-000156.life: Born in 1506 in the kingdom of Navarre, Francis Xavier became a friend of Ignatius of Loyola and one of the first seven Jesuits. In 1542 he reached Goa and spent the next decade carrying the gospel through India, the Malay world, the Moluccas and Japan. He learned to adapt to local languages and customs and urged the training of native clergy. Britannica credits him with some thirty thousand baptisms. He died of fever on 3 December 1552 on Sancian Island, within sight of China, which he had longed to enter. He is remembered as the Apostle of the Indies.
UO-SIN-000156.place: Navarre; Goa, India; Japan; Sancian Island, China

UO-SIN-000157.name: John of Damascus
UO-SIN-000157.life: John was born in Damascus around 675, into a Christian family that served the Umayyad caliphs, and he began as a government official like his father. Around 730 he retreated to the monastery of Mar Saba near Jerusalem, where he was ordained and spent his remaining years writing and preaching. When the Byzantine emperor Leo III banned holy images, John wrote three famous defences of icons from beyond the emperor's reach. His great work, the Fountain of Knowledge, gathered the teaching of the Fathers into one system, and he also wrote hymns still sung in the East. He died about 749.

UO-SIN-000158.name: Clement of Alexandria
UO-SIN-000158.life: Born around 150, probably in Athens, to pagan parents, Clement travelled widely in search of teachers before coming to Christ and settling in Alexandria. There he studied under Pantaenus and later led the city's Christian school, teaching for roughly two decades. His surviving works, the Exhortation to the Greeks, the Instructor and the Miscellanies, argue that the best of Greek philosophy prepared the way for the gospel and that the Christian is called to a life of reasoned, loving devotion. Persecution under Severus drove him from Egypt about 202, and he died in Palestine around 215. Origen was among those he influenced.

UO-SIN-000159.name: Nicholas of Myra
UO-SIN-000159.life: Little is known for certain about Nicholas, who was probably bishop of Myra, in Lycia on the south coast of Asia Minor, in the fourth century. According to tradition he was born at Patara to wealthy parents and gave away his inheritance to the poor. The best-loved story tells how he secretly tossed bags of gold into a poor man's house so that three daughters could marry. Other tales have him calming storms and rescuing the innocent, which made him patron of sailors and children. His relics were carried off to Bari in Italy in 1087. From Dutch Sinterklaas, his name gave rise to Santa Claus.

UO-SIN-000160.name: Ambrose of Milan
UO-SIN-000160.life: Ambrose was born about 339 at Trier in what is now Germany. In 374 the people of Milan acclaimed him their bishop, though he was newly baptized and had no theological training. As bishop he defended the Nicene faith against the Arians, wrote sermons, treatises and hymns, and taught that an emperor belongs within the church, not over it, even calling Theodosius to penance after the massacre at Thessalonica. His preaching helped lead Augustine to baptism. Ambrose died in Milan in 397.

UO-SIN-000161.name: Nicholas Ferrar
UO-SIN-000161.life: Born in London in 1592, Nicholas Ferrar studied medicine in Europe, and he invested in the Virginia Company, losing his fortune. After a brief spell in Parliament in 1624, he left public life. In 1626 he settled with his extended family at Little Gidding in Huntingdonshire, was ordained deacon, and led a household of daily prayer, charity to the neighbours, teaching of local children, and fine bookbinding and Gospel harmonies. He saw George Herbert's poems through the press as The Temple in 1633. Ferrar died at Little Gidding in 1637. T. S. Eliot later gave the place its place in modern poetry.

UO-SIN-000162.name: Juan Diego
